opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think three-to-one is some magic number. It's more of an empirical sweet spot that a lot of groups landed on independently, and then it became a convention.

Pure linear attention models, even good ones like the gated DeltaNet family, compress the whole history into a fixed-size state. That's great for efficiency, but it hurts on tasks that need precise retrieval: needle-in-a-haystack, copying, in-context recall over long documents. The state is just a lossy memory. So you need some full-attention layers to do exact lookup over the KV cache.

The question is how many. When people sweep the ratio, the curve is pretty flat across a range. Going from all softmax attention to something like one full-attention layer in every four, you lose very little on language modeling and recall benchmarks. Sometimes the hybrid is even slightly better, because the linear layers give you a nice recurrent inductive bias and positional information for free. But if you push much further, to one in eight or one in sixteen, retrieval-heavy tasks start to degrade noticeably, especially at long context.

Then there's the systems side. With three-to-one, the KV cache is roughly a quarter of a full Transformer's, and the attention compute at long context drops by a similar factor. That's already a big win for inference and long-context serving. Going more aggressive gives diminishing returns on efficiency, since other costs start to dominate, while the quality risk keeps going up. So three-to-one sits at a comfortable point on the trade-off curve.

There's also a practical reason. Once a few strong models shipped with roughly that ratio and showed they could match full-attention baselines at scale, it became the safe default. Pretraining runs are expensive, and nobody wants to be the one who bet on one-to-seven and found a retrieval regression after spending millions of GPU hours.

But I'd stress that the optimal ratio depends on how strong your linear layer is. As linear attention gets more expressive, with better state updates, better gating, and maybe larger states, I'd expect the ratio to shift toward fewer full-attention layers. Where you place those layers, and whether some of them use sliding windows or sparse attention, also matters. So I see three-to-one as a snapshot of where the field is today, not a fundamental law.

r001.rationale: The response says one-in-eight or one-in-sixteen ratios cause retrieval-heavy tasks to degrade, and specifically describes betting on one-in-seven as risking a retrieval regression.

r002.rationale: It describes three-to-one as an empirical sweet spot and convention, but does not attribute that finding to Ziji or say it came from experiments training hybrid architectures from scratch.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's partly empirical and partly a story we tell afterward to explain the empirics.

The empirical part is fairly consistent across groups. If you look at Jamba, at Zamba, at what MiniMax did with Lightning Attention, at the Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear work, and at a lot of our own ablations with Gated DeltaNet, you see the same curve. You start from pure linear attention, you add a few full-attention layers, and the quality jump from zero to a handful of softmax layers is enormous. Retrieval tasks, needle-in-a-haystack, in-context learning, anything that needs exact token-level lookup, all of it recovers very quickly. Then the curve flattens. Going from one-in-four to one-in-two full attention buys you very little on most benchmarks, but it roughly halves the memory and throughput advantage you got from going linear in the first place. So three-to-one sits right at the knee of that curve. It's not a magic number, it's where the marginal benefit stops paying for the marginal cost.

The story we tell afterward is about division of labor. Linear attention, especially the delta-rule variants, is a fixed-size state that gets updated recurrently. It's good at compressing the sequence into a summary and doing associative recall when the key is approximately right. It's bad at precise, sparse, long-range lookup, because the state has finite capacity and old information gets overwritten. Softmax attention is the opposite. It has unbounded memory in the form of the KV cache, and it can attend to one exact token from a hundred thousand positions ago. So you don't actually need very many of those layers. You need enough that information can be fetched precisely a few times through the depth of the network, and then the linear layers can process and propagate it. One full-attention layer every four blocks gives you that routing capacity without paying for it everywhere.

There are also some practical reasons that get less attention. With three-to-one, the KV cache for a long-context model shrinks by roughly four times, which changes what batch sizes you can run at inference and what hardware you can serve on. And from a training-systems perspective, having the layers interleaved at a regular period makes pipeline and tensor parallelism simpler than an irregular pattern would.

That said, I would be careful about treating it as settled. The right ratio depends on the linear layer you're using. A weak linear layer, something like plain linear attention without gating or the delta rule, needs more softmax layers to compensate. A stronger recurrent layer with better state management can probably tolerate a sparser ratio, and some of the recent work is already pushing toward seven-to-one or even more aggressive settings with sliding-window attention mixed in. It also depends on what you're optimizing for. If your workload is dominated by long-context retrieval, you might want more full attention. If it's dominated by throughput, less. Three-to-one is the current default because it's a good compromise across the tasks people usually evaluate on, but I expect it to drift as the linear layers improve and as we understand better exactly what the softmax layers are contributing.

r001.rationale: The response mentions work exploring seven-to-one ratios and says long-context retrieval may call for more full attention, but it does not clearly connect seven-to-one to too few softmax layers for strong long-context performance.

r002.rationale: The response describes empirical results and its own ablations, but does not report Ziji’s from-scratch experiments or attribute the approximately optimal three-to-one ratio to them.

astra-6.text:
I think three-to-one is a practical sweet spot, rather than a fundamental rule. Linear attention lets you process most layers with lower cost, especially as the context gets longer. But it compresses the history into a fixed-size state, so preserving and retrieving specific details can be challenging. Full attention gives the model opportunities to look directly at earlier tokens.

With three linear-attention layers followed by one full-attention layer, you get much of the efficiency benefit while regularly restoring that direct access to the context. Adding more full-attention layers may give you diminishing quality gains relative to their memory and compute cost; using fewer may hurt tasks that depend on precise retrieval.

But I wouldn’t say three-to-one must be optimal. The best ratio depends on the particular linear-attention mechanism, the model size, the training setup, and the tasks you care about. It’s an empirical design choice, and the placement of those full-attention layers can matter as well as their number.

sol-6.1.text:
I think three-to-one is a practical sweet spot, rather than a fundamental rule. Linear attention gives you an efficient way to process most of the sequence, while periodic full-attention layers let the model directly access individual tokens and recover details that a compressed state might lose.

If you use too much full attention, you give up much of the efficiency benefit. If you use too little, tasks that need precise retrieval or complex interactions across the context can suffer. Three-to-one is a reasonable balance between those two pressures.

But I’d be careful about calling it universally optimal. The best ratio depends on the linear-attention mechanism, model size, context length, training setup, and even the hardware. It’s an empirical design choice, and the placement of the full-attention layers can matter as much as the ratio itself.
